story.lead: The ferry is busiest on summer weekend middays
story.summary: The Island ferry peaks in August, on a Saturday, around noon. On an average August day, **9,768** people board a ferry to the islands. In an average January, it is only **492**, about one-twentieth of that. The charts below go from the busiest month, to the busiest day, to the busiest hour.
story.sub: Ferry tickets used, 15-minute counts for complete years 2016-2025.

facts.label: average riders on an August day
average riders on a summer Saturday
average riders between noon and 1 pm in summer

points.h: Summer is the season, and August is the peak
points.p: The ferry's year looks like a tall hill. Winter days are quiet, with **492** riders a day in January and **607** in December. Numbers climb through spring and reach **8,699** a day in July and **9,768** in August. August is about twenty times busier than January. By September the daily number has already halved to **4,959**.

points.h: Weekends bring about twice the crowds
points.p: Within summer, the day of the week matters a lot. Saturday is the busiest day with **12,513** riders, and Sunday follows with **11,518**. Tuesday is the quietest at **5,521**. A summer Saturday has more than twice as many riders as a Tuesday. Friday, at **7,257**, is the busiest of the weekdays.

points.h: Within a day, the crowd peaks around noon
points.p: Finally, the time of day. On an average summer day, almost nobody boards early: just **51** riders from 7 to 8 am and **126** from 8 to 9 am. Boardings then build quickly, and the busiest hour is noon to 1 pm, with **995** riders. The hours from 10 am to 2 pm are all above **800**. After the early afternoon the crowd thins steadily, to **341** at 6 pm and **76** at 9 pm.

story.takeaway: Put the three together and the busiest time is a summer weekend, with August the best bet, and the crowd peaking around midday. If you want a quieter trip, go on a weekday morning or evening, or outside the summer months.
story.note: Figures count tickets used, which is people boarding a ferry to the islands, averaged over 2016-2025.

story.lead: Kipling station has the most subway delays
story.summary: Kipling station, at the western end of the Bloor-Danforth line, had more delays than any other subway station: **578** between January 2025 and August 2026. Kennedy (**537**), Wilson (**513**) and Bloor (**504**) were close behind. But the busiest list changes when you count minutes instead of incidents. Eglinton lost the most time, **4,001 minutes**, and a different set of stations has the longest delays one by one.

facts.label: delays at Kipling station, the most of any station

points.h: Kipling and Kennedy top the list for delays
points.p: Start with the simplest count: how often trains were held up. Kipling leads with **578** delays, followed by Kennedy with **537** and Wilson with **513**. Bloor (**504**), Finch (**464**) and Eglinton (**446**) complete the top six. After that the numbers drop: Davisville is seventh with **336**, well below the leaders.

points.h: Add up the minutes and Eglinton comes first
points.p: Counting incidents is only half the story, because some delays last far longer than others. Add up the minutes and Eglinton moves to the top with **4,001** minutes, even though it ranks sixth by number of delays. Kipling is second with **3,461** minutes and Kennedy third with **3,136**. Some stations jump up the list: Victoria Park (**3,097**) and Sheppard West (**3,096**) were not among the top six for number of delays. Those two had fewer incidents but long ones.

points.h: Some stations have fewer but longer delays
points.p: This chart looks at how long a typical delay lasts, only for stations with at least 30 delays. Woodbine tops it with **12.3 minutes** per delay, then Sheppard West at **12** and Islington at **11.9**. Victoria Park (**11.7**) also appears, which fits its high total of minutes. Eglinton averages **9** minutes per delay, so its place at the top for lost time comes from having both many delays and fairly long ones.

story.takeaway: Which station is worst depends on how you measure. Kipling has the most delays, Eglinton has lost the most time, and Woodbine has the longest delay on average. Eglinton and Kipling rank near the top in both counts and minutes.
story.note: Only delays of more than zero minutes are counted, and the data covers 1 January 2025 to 31 August 2026.

story.lead: Electrical failure is the top known cause of fires
story.summary: The most common answer in Toronto's fire records is "undetermined": **4,012** fires have no clear cause. Of the causes that are known, electrical failure comes first, with **3,134** fires from 2011 to 2024. Next come materials that were improperly discarded (**2,255**) and things left unattended (**1,928**). But when we count people hurt rather than fires, a different cause comes out on top.
story.sub: Based on fires Toronto Fire Services attended, 2011 to 2024 (fires only, not outdoor no-loss fires).

facts.label: fires with an undetermined cause, the largest group
fires caused by electrical failure, top known cause
civilian casualties from unattended fires, the most of any cause

points.h: No one could say what started the most fires
points.p: Start with the full list of recorded causes. The biggest single entry is not a cause at all: **4,012** fires are listed as undetermined. Electrical failure is second with **3,134** fires, then improperly discarded materials with **2,255**. Many of the next entries are broad labels such as "other unintended cause" and "not classified", so a lot of fires fall into loose groups.

points.h: Take out the unknowns, and electrical failure leads
points.p: Remove the fires with unknown causes and the picture gets clearer. Electrical failure stays on top with **3,134** fires, about **1.4 times** as many as improperly discarded materials (**2,255**). Unattended fires follow with **1,928**, and misuse of an ignition source or of the material that caught fire has **1,382**. Even the twelfth cause on the list, intentional fires, still has **617** fires.

points.h: Unattended fires hurt the most people
points.p: Counting fires is not the same as counting harm. Here the cause is ranked by the number of civilians hurt or killed, and unattended fires come out first with **350** casualties. That is more than twice the next cause, improper handling of an ignition source or of what was ignited, at **170**. Electrical failure is third with **164**. So the most common cause is not the one that hurts the most people.

story.takeaway: Electrical failure starts the most fires with a known cause, and many fires have no known cause at all. Unattended fires are fewer, yet they hurt the most people.
story.note: Casualties in the last chart cover all recorded fires, not only home fires, and leave out fires coded "99 - Undetermined" (the separate "unintentional, cause undetermined" code is still included).

story.summary: On an average night in 2024, **9,766** people stayed in a Toronto shelter. That was the highest yearly figure in the data, up from **6,382** in 2021. Since then the number has come down, and in 2026 it averages **8,209** a night. The charts below show the climb, the recent drop and who is using shelters.

points.h: Up for three years, then down
points.p: The yearly picture starts with a steep climb. The nightly average rose from **6,382** in 2021 to **9,766** in 2024, an increase of about half. Then it turned. It was **9,215** in 2025 and **8,209** so far in 2026. That is about 1,550 fewer people a night than at the peak.

points.h: The drop continues, apart from small winter bumps
points.p: The monthly view shows the fall is still going. points.h: Mixed adult shelters and families make up most of it

Women averaged **1,082** and youth **719**. Together, Mixed Adult and Families made up more than half of the nightly total.

story.takeaway: Shelter use grew quickly from 2021 to 2024, then began to fall, and the fall is still under way. The latest months are the lowest in the two years shown. Mixed adult and family programs hold the most people.

story.lead: Gibraltar Point Beach is the safest for swimming.
story.summary: Gibraltar Point Beach had the cleanest water of Toronto's ten beaches since 2021. On only **4.3%** of the days it was tested was the water unsafe, meaning E. coli (a germ that shows sewage pollution) was above the City's limit of 100. Sunnyside Beach was unsafe on **36.8%** of days, about nine times as often. Next, we look at how often each beach failed, how much germ was typical, and how much testing backs this up.
story.sub: Based on daily E. coli tests at 10 Toronto beaches, swimming seasons 2021 to 2026.

facts.label: Days unsafe at Gibraltar Point Beach
Days unsafe at Sunnyside Beach, the worst
Days tested at Gibraltar Point Beach

points.h: Four beaches are unsafe on fewer than one day in ten
points.p: The most direct test of safety is how often a beach goes over the limit. Gibraltar Point Beach was unsafe on **4.3%** of days, followed by Hanlan's Point Beach at **6.6%** and Cherry Beach at **7.7%**. Ward's Island Beach was close behind at 9.8%. At the other end, Centre Island Beach, Marie Curtis Park East Beach and Sunnyside Beach were each unsafe on more than a third of days. So the gap between the best and worst beaches is large.

points.h: On a typical day, the top four are equally clean
points.p: A beach can pass most days and still have bad spells, so we also checked the middle value. The middle reading is the level that half of all days fall below. Gibraltar Point, Hanlan's Point, Ward's Island and Cherry Beach all share the lowest middle level, at **14** E. coli per 100 mL. That is far under the limit of 100. Sunnyside Beach had the highest middle level at **74**, about five times higher. Gibraltar Point wins on how rarely it fails, but the other three are very close on a normal day.

points.h: Every beach has about 600 days of testing behind it
points.p: Do these results rest on enough tests? Each beach was sampled on between **601** and **651** days since 2021. Gibraltar Point Beach had the fewest of the ten, at 601, which is still plenty. The ranking is built on similar amounts of testing at every beach, so the comparison is fair.

story.takeaway: Gibraltar Point Beach is the safest pick because its water was over the limit least often. Hanlan's Point, Cherry Beach and Ward's Island are close behind. Sunnyside, Centre Island and Marie Curtis Park East were the most likely to be unsafe.
story.note: Unsafe means a daily average above 100 E. coli per 100 mL, the City's posting level, and only swimming-season test days are counted.

story.lead: Pothole complaints hit a record in 2026
story.summary: Toronto has never had this many pothole complaints, and 2026 isn't over yet. In just the first eight months, 311 logged **23,976** pothole requests. That is more than any full year since 2019, and about **twice** the 11,718 of all of 2025. Below, you'll see the yearly ups and downs, the time of year when potholes get reported, and how sharply this winter and spring stood out.

facts.label: pothole requests, Jan–Aug 2026

points.h: Complaints bounce around, then 2026 jumps off the chart
points.p: Pothole complaints have never moved in a straight line. They fell from **18,495** in 2019 to a low of **4,432** in 2021, climbed to 15,578 in 2023, then dropped again to 6,948 in 2024. After 11,718 in 2025, 2026 has already reached **23,976** with four months still to count. That is about 5.4 times the 2021 low and well above the 2019 high.

points.h: Potholes get reported in late winter, not summer
points.p: The calendar shows when in the year complaints come in. In an average year, March is the peak with about **2,706** requests, while November is the quietest with about **359**. That makes March roughly seven and a half times busier. February, March and April together make up about half of a typical year's complaints.

points.h: This winter and spring were far worse than last year's
points.p: The last 24 months show how the 2026 record was built. February 2026 had **5,067** requests, about four times the 1,244 of February 2025. March 2026 hit **6,227**, nearly double March 2025's 3,250. February to April 2026 alone brought in about two thirds of the year's total so far. By August 2026, the gap had nearly closed: 629 requests against 563 a year before.

story.takeaway: Pothole complaints rise and fall from year to year, and they always peak in late winter. In 2026 that peak was much bigger than usual, which is why the year already has more requests than any full year in the data.
story.note: 2026 only covers January to August, so its final total will be higher still. Since 2025 the main pothole request type has been named "Road Pothole / Road Damage", so it may include some road damage that was not counted as potholes before.

story.lead: Closures after inspection are very rare in Toronto
story.summary: Out of more than 80,000 restaurant and food shop inspections, only **82** ended with the place being closed. That is about **1 in 1,000**. points.h: Closures happen a few times a month at most

story.lead: Toronto Fire typically arrives in about five minutes.
story.summary: When Toronto Fire is called, the first truck typically arrives in about **5 minutes**. That has barely moved in seven years: the typical time was **4.9 minutes** in 2018 and **5.1 minutes** in 2024. Fires and medical calls, the most urgent kinds, sit at the quick end at **5 minutes**. The night hours are a little slower than the day.

facts.label: Typical response time in 2024

points.h: The typical wait has hardly changed in seven years
points.p: Start with the big picture. The typical response time was **4.9 minutes** in both 2018 and 2019. It crept up to a high of **5.3 minutes** in 2022. Then it eased back to **5.1 minutes** in 2023 and 2024. Over the whole period, the typical wait moved by less than half a minute.

points.h: Fires and medical calls get the fastest response
points.p: The time also depends on what kind of call it is. Emergency fire and medical calls both have a typical time of **5 minutes**, the quickest of any type. Vehicle incidents take **5.5 minutes**, and carbon monoxide and hazardous materials calls take **6 minutes**. Non-emergency calls come last at **7.4 minutes**, about two and a half minutes slower than fires. The most urgent calls get the quickest arrival.

points.h: Nights are slower than days
points.p: The time of day matters too. From 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. the typical time stays at **4.9 or 5 minutes**. It starts to rise late in the evening, to **5.3 minutes** at 11 p.m. Between 3 and 5 a.m. it reaches **5.8 minutes**, the slowest of the day. Even then, the difference from the daytime is under one minute.

story.takeaway: Toronto Fire usually gets a truck to the door in about five minutes, and that has held steady since 2018. Urgent fire and medical calls are the quickest, and the small slowdowns come at night and for non-emergency calls.
story.note: These are typical (median) times, so half of calls were faster and half slower. Individual calls can take much longer.

story.lead: Permits added 87,600 homes, mostly in big buildings
story.summary: Building permits cleared since 2017 created about **87,600** new homes in Toronto between 2017 and 2025. Most of them came in the first five years, with a peak of **15,109** in 2021. By 2025 the yearly count had fallen to **2,063**, about one-seventh of the peak. Below, we look at the yearly count, what is left after homes are lost, and which kinds of buildings make up the total.
story.sub: Building permits cleared (closed or finished), issued January 2017 to December 2025.

facts.label: new homes from permits issued, 2017–2025
homes created in the peak year, 2021

points.h: Homes created rose to 2021, then fell sharply
points.p: The yearly count started at **9,163** homes in 2017. It climbed to **14,184** in 2020 and **15,109** in 2021. Then it dropped to **8,718** in 2022 and **9,311** in 2023. By 2024 it was **4,180**, and 2025 was lower again at **2,063**. That is about seven times fewer than in 2021.

points.h: Counting homes lost, the picture is the same
points.p: Some permits also remove homes, so this chart subtracts them. The pattern does not change. Net new homes peaked at **13,565** in 2021 and fell to **1,363** in 2025. Over the nine years, about **10,953** homes were lost, leaving a net gain of roughly **76,686**. Losses were small next to the homes created, so they do not explain the drop.

points.h: Mixed-use and apartment buildings account for most homes
points.p: What kind of building holds all these new homes? The biggest group is mixed-use buildings, with homes above shops or offices, at **39,798**. Apartment buildings come next at **28,518**. Together they hold **68,316** homes. Detached houses add only **6,073**, so mixed-use buildings gave about **seven times** as many homes. Smaller types, such as two-unit houses (**3,330**), townhouses (**2,071**) and laneway suites (**921**), fill in the rest.

story.takeaway: Permits created tens of thousands of homes, and about four in five of them were in apartment and mixed-use buildings. The yearly count peaked in 2021 and was far lower by 2025. Losses of homes were small by comparison.
story.note: Only permits already closed or finished are counted, so the low numbers for 2024 and 2025 may not be the full picture of what was approved in those years.

story.lead: Garbage bins are the top reason people call 311
story.summary: The biggest reason Torontonians contact 311 is trouble with household garbage and bins. Broken bin lids lead the list, with about **138,600** requests since 2019 once the old and new names are added together. Across all 311 requests, the garbage and recycling division handles **36%**, more than any other part of the City. Next we look at the single most common requests, then the bigger picture by division, then the most recent full year.
story.sub: 311 service requests, January 2019 to August 2026, with a closer look at 2025.

facts.label: of all 311 requests go to garbage and recycling

points.h: Broken bin lids top the list of single requests
points.p: Start with the most common individual requests. "Repair or Replace Lid" comes first with **101,371** requests. The City renamed this request in 2025, and the new name, "Residential Bin Lid Damaged", adds another **37,270**, so the two together come to about **138,600**. Property standards complaints are next with **81,495**, then injured wildlife with **73,186**. Missed pickups of garbage, furniture, green bins and recycling fill much of the rest of the list.

points.h: Three City divisions handle most of the calls
points.p: Renamed requests make the list above hard to read, so this chart groups calls by the City division that handles them. Division names did not change. Solid waste, the garbage and recycling service, received **1,133,635** of about **3.1 million** requests, or **36%**. Roads and sidewalks (Transportation Services) had **800,318**, and licensing and standards had **749,891**. Those three divisions together account for **86%** of all requests.

points.h: In 2025, bin lids still came first
points.p: The most recent full year shows the same picture under the new names. "Residential Bin Lid Damaged" led with **24,448** requests, about **1.4 times** the next type, property standards violations at **17,079**. Wildlife was close behind: **15,513** requests to pick up dead animals and **15,192** about injured ones. Missed pickups of garbage, recycling and green bins add up to **25,537** requests, a little more than bin lids alone. Everyday waste problems still make up much of what people call about.

story.takeaway: People call 311 most about the basics of living in a city: bins that break, garbage that is not picked up, and animals found hurt or dead. One in three requests goes to the garbage and recycling division, and bin lids were still the top request in 2025.
story.note: The City renamed many request types in 2025, so the first chart counts old and new names separately, and I added the two bin lid names together by hand.

points.h: Two buildings sit far below all the rest

story.lead: Coyote calls have nearly doubled in two years
story.summary: Toronto's Animal Services answered **5,399** coyote requests in 2025. That is almost twice the **2,781** in 2023. This year is not over, and it already has **3,837** requests. The city's 311 phone line tells the same story, and the charts below show it year by year and month by month.
story.sub: Animal Services requests 2023 to 2026 and 311 requests 2019 to 2026 (2026 is a part year, data downloaded 5 Oct 2026).

facts.label: coyote requests to Animal Services in 2025

points.h: Animal Services coyote requests jumped in 2025
points.p: Start with the team that responds to these calls. Animal Services had **2,781** coyote requests in 2023 and **3,088** in 2024. In 2025 the number leapt to **5,399**, about 1.75 times the year before. The part-year total for 2026 is already **3,837**, about 71% of the whole of 2025.

points.h: The 311 line shows the same climb, over a longer time
points.p: The city's 311 line goes back further, and it shows this is not a one-year blip. Coyote requests were **127** in 2019 and fell to **88** in 2021. Then they rose every year: **162**, **226**, **365**, and **498** in 2025. That is about four times the 2019 level. The 2026 total up to August is already **369**, about three quarters of the 2025 total.

points.h: Calls come in all year, with a bump in summer and autumn
points.p: Is this a seasonal thing? Not much. Adding up 2019 to 2025, every month had at least **101** requests. July was busiest with **173**, and June was lowest with **101**. November (**168**) and October (**151**) were also high. So coyote calls are a year-round matter, with a modest lift in the later months.

story.takeaway: Both sources point the same way: coyote requests have risen every year since 2021 on the 311 line and since 2023 at Animal Services. The rise is steepest since 2024, and this year is already near last year's total. The calls are spread across the whole year, not just one season.
story.note: The two sources count different things and cannot be added together: Animal Services counts its response requests, and 311 counts calls to the city line.

story.lead: Serious collisions peak in the early evening
story.summary: Across Toronto, more serious collisions happen at 6 pm than at any other hour. Of the 7,620 collisions where someone was killed or seriously hurt, **531** happened between 6 and 7 pm. That is more than six times as many as in the quietest hour, 4 am. Fridays and the warm months of June to October are also busier than the rest of the week and year.
story.sub: Based on collisions where someone was killed or seriously injured, 2006 to September 2026.

facts.label: serious collisions in the busiest hour, 6 pm
happen between 3 pm and 8 pm
happen in the five months June to October

points.h: The afternoon and evening are the danger zone
points.p: The day starts quiet. Collisions fall to just **84** at 4 am, then climb through the morning to around 300 an hour by 9 am. They keep rising all afternoon and reach their top at 6 pm, with **531**. Five hours, from 3 pm to 8 pm, hold 2,379 collisions, or about **31%** of all of them. After 8 pm the numbers ease down again through the night.

points.h: Fridays are worst, Sundays are calmest
points.p: The week is much flatter than the day. Friday is the highest with **1,216** collisions, and Sunday is the lowest with **966**. That makes Friday about a quarter busier than Sunday. Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday sit close together, between 1,092 and 1,138. So the time of day matters far more than the day of the week.

points.h: Summer and autumn bring the most collisions
points.p: The year has a clear shape too. February is the quietest month with **455** collisions, and June is the busiest with **774**, about 1.7 times as many. The five months from June to October add up to 3,752 collisions, or roughly **half** of the total. May to October all run above 630. So serious collisions cluster in the warmer part of the year.

story.takeaway: Serious collisions are most common on a Friday evening in early autumn or summer, around the end of the working day. Time of day shows the biggest swing, the season a moderate one, and the day of the week the smallest.
story.note: Each collision is counted once, however many people were involved, and all years from 2006 to 2026 are added together.
